chief_complaint: mild left lower abdominal pain and constipation for 3 days
hpi_details: A 35-year-old male presents to the clinic with mild left lower abdominal pain and constipation for 3 days. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks being severely backed up caused hard stool to get physically trapped in the left side of his colon and become sore.
concerns: He is worried that his intestine might burst and force him into emergency surgery, making him miss his sister's wedding this weekend.
expectations: He hopes to get a gentle laxative to clear his bowels and an imaging scan to verify that his colon is not torn.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Diverticulitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

For uncomplicated diverticulitis in an immunocompetent, clinically stable patient, supportive care and close follow-up are often appropriate; use antibiotics selectively, and use CT when the diagnosis is uncertain or complications are suspected.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Acute Diverticulitis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Diverticulitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Colorectal cancer without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Worsening pain with a rigid or increasingly tender abdomen — suggests perforation.
management_principles: Assess severity and complications; use CT when diagnosis is uncertain or complications are suspected, and reserve antibiotics for selected higher-risk or complicated presentations
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 35-year-old male presents with a 3-day history of mild left lower quadrant abdominal pain and constipation, without fever or peritonism.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Acute Diverticulitis.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis. DDx: colorectal cancer, ischaemic colitis, inflammatory bowel disease.
reference_soap.plan: Assess for peritonitis, systemic illness, immunocompromise, and inability to tolerate oral intake. Obtain CT when diagnosis is uncertain or complications are suspected. For mild uncomplicated disease in an immunocompetent patient, use supportive care and close follow-up; prescribe antibiotics selectively for higher-risk or complicated disease.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Acute Diverticulitis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Acute Diverticulitis
Implement evidence-based management plan: severity assessment, selective CT, and selective antibiotic use

teaching.one_liner: Small pouches in the colon wall become inflamed, causing steady left-lower-quadrant pain and constipation.
red_flags: Worsening pain with a rigid or increasingly tender abdomen — suggests perforation

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, pulse 74 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Abdomen is flat and symmetrical without distension, visible pulsations, or surgical scars.
Bowel sounds are slightly hypoactive but audible across all four quadrants, with no abdominal bruits heard.
Mild localized tenderness upon deep palpation in the left lower quadrant; abdomen is soft with no involuntary guarding or palpable mass.
No rebound tenderness elicited in any quadrant.
No right lower quadrant tenderness at McBurney point; psoas and obturator signs are negative.
Inspiratory arrest test is negative without right upper quadrant tenderness.
Normal sphincter tone without palpable masses or focal rectal tenderness; brown stool without visible blood on the glove.
